q: What is the net floor area of the room 'KORIDOR (119)' on '1.korrus', in m²?
note: Area from the IFC model, shown on the drawing and in 3D: same room, same GlobalId.

q: How many doors are shown on the floor plan of '1.korrus'?
note: Count with one box per door. The drawing and the model agree (cross-check), no model call needed.

q: How many windows are shown on the floor plan of '1.korrus'?
note: Windows: the model has 55 on this storey, the drawing shows 52. The cross-check explains the gap instead of hiding it: the plan is a cut at floor + 1.2 m, and 3 windows lie entirely above or below it (see the highlighted check below).

q: How many doors are there in the model 'Maleva tänav 18 korterelamu (Esplanades example model)'?
note: Model-wide question: evidence on five sheets. Click a sheet chip to open it.

q: If each door costs 450 euros, what do all the doors on '1.korrus' cost in total?
note: A question no template covers, with a number in it. The IFC rules read 'each door costs 450 €' as a factor, count the 46 doors on the storey and multiply in code: 46 × 450 € = 20,700 €, every door boxed, no language model call, 0.2 s. Questions the rules cannot read go to a small local model that plans tool calls; the numbers still come from the tools.

q: What plumbing fixtures are in this building and their respective counts?
note: A free-text question about a Revit model. A local model answers from facts extracted from the IFC, then the browser counts every fixture type it names in the loaded model (no model call). The card leads with that table: 4 types, 21 fixtures, each count ✓, highlighted in 3D (orange). Fixtures of the same kind that an answer leaves out would be listed ✗ and shown in purple.

q: How many doors (interior doors and entrance doors together) are drawn on this floor plan?
note: Vector drawing: doors counted on the CAD layer and mapped back onto the PDF.

q: Wie viele Türen und Fenster sind insgesamt auf diesem Grundriss eingezeichnet?
note: A German question that combines two counts: it is split into two sub-questions, each answered and cross-checked, and the sum is done in code.

A Finnish apartment plan, asked in Finnish: our fine-tuned 8B vision model (LoRA) counts 3 bedrooms. To keep cost low it reads no boxes itself; 'Show where' asks a second reader for the room names, it finds the three 'MH' labels, they agree (✓), and each counted bedroom is marked.

q: How many saunas are on this floor plan?
note: The fine-tuned model says 0 saunas at 82 %, with nothing to point at. 'Show where' asks the label reader, which finds 'LH' (löylyhuone, the sauna room): the card turns the disagreement into a ✗ and marks the label. One glance shows the sauna: this is how a person catches a confident wrong answer in seconds.

q: What kind of drawing is this (floor plan, elevation, section, site plan)?
note: Historical scan (HAER, 1977): no digital text at all. The local vision model reads the printed text tile by tile and answers from it, citing the lines it used: the title 'NORTH ELEVATION' is boxed on the sheet. NVIDIA Nemotron (hosted, one paid call) gives a second opinion. Below: the other sheets of the same survey, linked.

Helsinki Olympic Stadium, site plan (Lindegren & Jäntti; Architecture & Design Museum, CC BY 4.0), asked in Finnish: 'what is the scale of the drawing?' The answer 1/500 is read from the hand-lettered note 'ASEMAPIIRROS M.K. 1/500', which is boxed. On scans, every answer points at the printed text it came from; local model only, no cloud call.
Measured on held-out drawings: accuracy per source against two baselines, generality, and cost per 1,000 questions.
